```{r knitr-setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    comment = "#",
    prompt = FALSE,
    tidy = FALSE,
    cache = FALSE,
    collapse = TRUE
)

old <- options(width = 100L)
```

[Get started](v01-get-started.html) built a document with one *layout step*:
a step that takes the outputs of other steps and arranges them with
`pub_doc()` and `pub_section()`. This vignette is about what comes with real
reports: inputs that fail, reports that show only some of the steps, a
number of sections that depends on the data, a report over several pipelines,
and how to test all of this. It builds on pipeflow's vignettes
[Pipeline views](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v03b-pipeline-views.html),
[Error handling](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v05c-error-handling.html)
and
[Split, map and reduce](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v05a-split-map-reduce.html).

```{r library}
library(pipeflow)
library(pubflow)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r show, include = FALSE}
# Shows a document in place, framed to set it apart from the vignette's own
# text, with its headings left out of the table of contents of the pkgdown site
show <- function(doc) {
    html <- pub_html(doc)
    htmltools::div(
        style = "border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 4px; padding: 0 1em;",
        htmltools::attachDependencies(
            htmltools::HTML(gsub("<h([1-6])", "<h\\1 data-toc-skip", html)),
            htmltools::htmlDependencies(html)
        )
    )
}
```

## The example

The pipeline of Get started again: `airquality` data, a linear model of the
ozone concentration and a table, a figure and a text made from the model.
The figure is made by a function defined outside the pipeline, which matters
for [the last section](#steps-that-make-figures).

```{r outputs}
coef_table <- function(model) {
    ci <- confint(model)
    coefs <- data.frame(
        term = rownames(ci),
        estimate = coef(model),
        lower = ci[, 1L],
        upper = ci[, 2L]
    )
    pub_table(
        coefs,
        caption = "Coefficients with 95% confidence limits",
        labels = c(
            term = "Term",
            estimate = "Estimate",
            lower = "Lower",
            upper = "Upper"
        ),
        digits = c(estimate = 3L, lower = 3L, upper = 3L)
    )
}

fit_figure <- function(model, data, xVar) {
    coefs <- coef(model)
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(.data[[xVar]], .data$Ozone)) +
        geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
        geom_abline(intercept = coefs[[1L]], slope = coefs[[2L]])
    pub_figure(p, caption = "Linear model fit", width = 6, height = 3.5)
}
```

```{r pipeline}
pip <- pip_new("ozone") |>
    pip_add("data", function(data = airquality) data) |>
    pip_add("prep", function(df = ~data) {
        df[, "Temp.Celsius"] <- (df[, "Temp"] - 32) * 5 / 9
        df
    }) |>
    pip_add("data_table", function(data = ~prep) {
        pub_table(
            head(data, 5L),
            caption = "The first rows of the data",
            digits = c(Temp.Celsius = 1L)
        )
    }) |>
    pip_add("fit", function(data = ~prep, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        lm(paste("Ozone ~", xVar), data = data)
    }) |>
    pip_add("coef_table", coef_table, params = list(model = ~fit)) |>
    pip_add("plot", function(model = ~fit, data = ~prep, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        fit_figure(model, data, xVar)
    }) |>
    pip_add("summary", function(model = ~fit) {
        pub_text(sprintf(
            "The model explains **%.0f%%** of the variance of the ozone concentration.",
            100 * summary(model)$r.squared
        ))
    })
```

`coef_table` is a function defined outside the pipeline and given to
`pip_add()` as it is. A function can't say `~fit` in its own signature, so
`params` connects its argument `model` to the step `fit`. The step `plot` shows the other way: an
inline function that only calls the outside one.

## Failures in a document

If a step fails, the steps that depend on it can't run. A report should still
show what is there, and say what is missing. That is the job of
`~try(step)` in a layout step: instead of skipping the layout step, pipeflow
hands it the *failure* of the input, and pubflow places it in the document as
an error box.

```{r layout-try}
pip |>
    pip_add(
        "report",
        function(
            table = ~ try(data_table),
            coefs = ~ try(coef_table),
            plot = ~ try(plot),
            summary = ~ try(summary)
        ) {
            pub_doc(
                pub_section("Data", table),
                pub_section("Results", summary, coefs, plot),
                title = "Ozone in New York"
            )
        }
    )
```

Make `fit` fail by asking for a variable that the data doesn't have. With
`on_error = "continue"` the run goes on with the steps that don't depend on
`fit`:

```{r failure-run}
pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Height"))
tryCatch(
    pip_run(pip, on_error = "continue", lgr = NULL),
    warning = function(w) cat(conditionMessage(w), "\n")
)
pip
```

The run warns (class `pipeflow_run_failed`), but the document is there. The
steps `coef_table`, `plot` and `summary` didn't run either, and each shows as
an error box that names the cause:

```{r failure-doc}
doc <- pip[["report", "out"]]
show(doc)
```

A Shiny app can show such a document while the user fixes a param. The viewer
(`pub_viewer_server()`) only renders the document that its `doc` reactive
returns; it never runs a pipeline. The app does that: it calls
`pip_run(on_error = "continue")` and passes the output of the layout step. A
few rules go with it:

* Write `~try()` for **every** input of a layout step that may arrive failed.
  If you forget it for one input, pipeflow skips the layout step after a
  failure of that input, and there is no document at all.
* Computation steps choose `~try()` per argument, as in any pipeline. Normally
  they take a plain `~step`, so they never see a failure object.
* A report file is different: `pub_render()` refuses a document with error
  items, so that a report with a hole in it is never published by accident.
  (The report spec of `pub_report_spec()` can allow them.) Run the pipeline
  of a report with the default `on_error = "stop"`; the failed step then
  stops the run and there is no document.

```{r render-refused, error = TRUE}
pub_render(doc, "docx")
```

Set the param back and the next run repairs the steps that failed:

```{r failure-repair}
pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Temp.Celsius"))
pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
pip
```

## Select the steps of a report by tags

A pipeline often has more outputs than one report shows. Tag the steps with
pipeflow's tags, then let the tags decide which steps a layout step uses.
`pub_layout_inputs()` returns the `~try(step)` references of a pipeline or of
a view on it, for a layout step whose function takes `...`:

```{r tags}
tagged <- pip_reset(pip_clone(pip))
pip_tag(pip_view(tagged, step = c("summary", "coef_table")), c("short", "long"))
pip_tag(pip_view(tagged, step = c("data_table", "plot")), "long")
```

Each report is a layout step with its own tag. Add them last, because the
steps are read when `pub_layout_inputs()` is called:

```{r tags-reports}
tagged |>
    pip_add(
        "short",
        \(...) pub_doc(list(...), title = "Short report"),
        params = pub_layout_inputs(pip_view(tagged, tags = "short"))
    ) |>
    pip_add(
        "long",
        \(...) pub_doc(list(...), title = "Long report"),
        params = pub_layout_inputs(pip_view(tagged, tags = "long"))
    )
```

`list(...)` is a named list, which becomes one section per step, titled by
the step's name. `unname(list(...))` places the outputs one after the other,
without sections. The reports share the steps, and a run of a view computes
just what its report needs:

```{r tags-run}
pip_run(pip_view(tagged, step = "short"), lgr = NULL)
tagged
show(tagged[["short", "out"]])
```

The steps `plot` and `data_table` are only needed by the long report and
did not run.

Tags are one way to select; every view works, e.g. one on the steps that directly
depend on `fit`: `pub_layout_inputs(pip_view(tagged, depends = "fit"))`.
(A view that contains partitioned steps, see below, and other steps needs
`exec = "reduce"` for the layout step; otherwise the layout step runs once per
partition.)

### One section per view

`pub_layout_sections()` makes a whole layout step with one section per view:
the section is titled by the name of the view and shows the outputs of its
steps in pipeline order. Here a tag selects the data section and the
dependency on `fit` the model section:

```{r sections}
sectioned <- pip_reset(pip_clone(pip))
pip_tag(pip_view(sectioned, step = "data_table"), "data")
pip_add(
    sectioned,
    "by_section",
    pub_layout_sections(list(
        Data = pip_view(sectioned, tags = "data"),
        Model = pip_view(sectioned, depends = "fit")
    ))
)
pip_run(sectioned, lgr = NULL)
show(sectioned[["by_section", "out"]])
```

A section whose outputs are all `NULL` is left out, so a step that a param
switches off returns `NULL`.

## Layouts that change with the data

The structure of a document often depends on the data: one section per batch,
per site, per month. Choose among three ways, from the simplest.

### A step that returns a named list

The step `monthly` returns one table for every month in the data. A named list
becomes one section per name when it is placed in a document, so the layout
step needs no code for the months. If the data change, the sections change
with them:

```{r named-list}
monthly_tables <- function(data) {
    months <- split(data, data$Month)
    names(months) <- month.name[as.integer(names(months))]
    lapply(months, \(d) {
        pub_table(
            data.frame(
                Variable = c("Ozone (ppb)", "Temperature (°C)"),
                Mean = c(mean(d$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE), mean(d$Temp.Celsius))
            ),
            caption = sprintf("Means in %s", month.name[d$Month[[1L]]]),
            digits = c(Mean = 1L)
        )
    })
}

p2 <- pip_clone(pip) |>
    pip_add("monthly", monthly_tables, params = list(data = ~prep)) |>
    pip_add("by_month", function(tables = ~ try(monthly)) {
        pub_doc(tables, title = "Means by month")
    })

pip_run(p2, lgr = NULL)
```

```{r named-list-show}
show(p2[["by_month", "out"]])
```

This is the right tool when the content of a section is a few outputs made
in one step. A step that returns a list is one step: if it fails, all
sections fail together, and the pipeline can't cache or re-run a single
section.

### Split steps: one partition per batch

If each batch needs its own chain of steps (a fit, a table and a figure per
batch), use pipeflow's split steps: a step with `exec = "split"` returns a
list, and every step downstream runs once per element, the *partitions*,
until a step with `exec = "reduce"` takes them all. A layout step downstream
of a split step runs once per partition and returns the section of that
partition. The step doesn't get the key of its partition, so the title comes
from the data:

```{r split}
ps <- pip_new("by-month") |>
    pip_add("data", function(data = airquality) {
        data$Temp.Celsius <- (data$Temp - 32) * 5 / 9
        data
    }) |>
    pip_add(
        "months",
        function(data = ~data) split(data, data$Month),
        exec = "split"
    ) |>
    pip_add("fit", function(data = ~months) lm(Ozone ~ Temp.Celsius, data = data)) |>
    pip_add("table", coef_table, params = list(model = ~fit)) |>
    pip_add("plot", function(model = ~fit, data = ~months) {
        fit_figure(model, data, "Temp.Celsius")
    }) |>
    pip_add("section", function(
        data = ~ try(months),
        table = ~ try(table),
        plot = ~ try(plot)
    ) {
        pub_section(month.name[data$Month[[1L]]], table, plot)
    })
```

A last step with `exec = "reduce"` gets the sections of all partitions as one
partitioned output and builds the document. `unname()` places the sections one
after the other; without it each partition becomes a sub-section titled by
its key, around the section the step returned:

```{r split-doc}
ps <- pip_add(
    ps,
    "doc",
    function(sections = ~ try(section)) {
        pub_doc(
            pub_section("Months", unname(sections)),
            title = "Ozone by month"
        )
    },
    exec = "reduce"
)
pip_run(ps, lgr = NULL)
ps
```

```{r split-show, echo = FALSE}
show(ps[["doc", "out"]])
```

Pipeflow's split steps fail per partition. If the table of one month fails,
its section shows an error box and the other months are complete. A failed
batch is also the only one that runs again in the next run, as long as the
failed step's params, exec mode and inputs are unchanged, no input ran again
and the run is not forced. Note that a param change outdates a whole step: all
its partitions run again, not only some.

Choose between the two like this: the named list is easiest if the content of
a section is made in one step. Split steps pay off when the chain per batch is
long, when it can fail, or when its results are expensive to recompute after a
failure. A
third way, *nested pipelines* (a pipeline that is a step function through
`as.function()`), is for batches that share one param set but are computed by
a pipeline of their own; see pipeflow's vignette
[Nested pipelines](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v05b-nested-pipeline.html).

### What does not work: add steps while running

A step that adds steps to the pipeline in the course of a run (a step
function that calls `pip_add(.self, ...)` for every batch it finds) does not
work for documents: the layout step can't name a step that does not exist when
it is added, because `pip_add()` rejects unknown `~step` references, and
`pub_layout_inputs()` lists the steps present at that moment. Use a named
list or a split step instead; both have as many outputs as there are batches.

```{r unknown-reference, error = TRUE}
pip_new("tmp") |>
    pip_add("report", function(table = ~ try(batch_a_table)) pub_doc(table))
```

## Documents across pipelines

Groups that have their own params, their own inputs or their own runs are
better as *independent pipelines* made by one constructor than as one
pipeline with partitions. A study can have one pipeline per test (assay,
water content, ...), each with its own specification limits, its own parameter
tab and its own run, possibly in a parallel worker. The report puts the parts
together.

A constructor for a group's pipeline. The layout step `content` makes the
part of the report for this group. It takes a plain `~table`, so it is skipped
when the table fails: the failure is handled where the parts are collected:

```{r group-constructor}
month_pipeline <- function(name, month) {
    pip_new(name) |>
        pip_add("data", function(data = airquality, month = 5L) {
            data[data$Month == month, ]
        }) |>
        pip_add("mean", function(data = ~data, limit = 40) {
            m <- mean(data$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE)
            if (is.nan(m)) stop("no ozone values")
            c(mean = m, limit = limit)
        }) |>
        pip_add("table", function(res = ~mean) {
            pub_table(
                data.frame(
                    Quantity = c("Mean ozone", "Limit"),
                    Value = unname(res)
                ),
                caption = "Ozone (ppb)",
                digits = c(Value = 1L)
            )
        }) |>
        pip_add("content", function(table = ~table) list(table)) |>
        pip_set_params(list(month = month))
}

pips <- list(
    May = month_pipeline("May", 5L),
    June = month_pipeline("June", 6L),
    July = month_pipeline("July", 7L)
)
```

Each group is run on its own. Here a loop runs them; an app can run each in a
parallel worker, which does the same and returns the pipeline:

```{r group-run}
for (p in pips) {
    pip_run(p, on_error = "continue", lgr = NULL)
}
pips$May
```

### Read the parts with `pub_out()`

The report takes the output of a group's layout step with `pub_out()`. It
differs from `p[["content", "out"]]` in one respect: it returns the output
only if the step is `done`. After a failed run a step keeps its *earlier*
output, so `p[[step, "out"]]` could silently put old results into a report.

```{r pub-out}
pub_out(pips$May, "content")
```

If the step is not done, `pub_out()` signals an error that names the pipeline
and the failed steps. With `on_error = "item"` it returns an error item
instead, which a document shows as an error box:

```{r pub-out-failed, error = TRUE}
pip_set_params(pips$June, list(month = 13L))
suppressWarnings(pip_run(pips$June, on_error = "continue", lgr = NULL))

pub_out(pips$June, "content")
```

### A report pipeline

A **report pipeline** puts the parts together. Its input step receives the
parts as a param value, a layout step builds the document, and the rest of
the report (cross-group tables, a summary of all groups) are ordinary steps of
this pipeline. pipeflow skips a param value that is `identical()` to the old
one, so parts that did not change don't outdate anything:

```{r report-pipeline}
report <- pip_new("report") |>
    pip_add("parts", function(parts = list()) parts) |>
    pip_add("doc", function(parts = ~ try(parts)) {
        pub_doc(pub_section("Ozone by month", parts), title = "Study report")
    })
```

The parts are a named list, so each group becomes a section titled by its
name. A group whose pipeline failed is shown as an error box in its section,
and the other groups' results are in the document:

```{r report-run}
parts <- lapply(pips, pub_out, step = "content", on_error = "item")
pip_set_params(report, list(parts = parts))
pip_run(report, lgr = NULL)
show(report[["doc", "out"]])
```

Repair the group and run the report pipeline again. The group's own run
re-runs only the steps that the param outdated, and the report pipeline
gets the new part:

```{r report-repair}
pip_set_params(pips$June, list(month = 6L))
pip_run(pips$June, lgr = NULL)
parts <- lapply(pips, pub_out, step = "content", on_error = "item")
pip_set_params(report, list(parts = parts))
pip_run(report, lgr = NULL)
report
```

Two things to know when a worker runs the group's pipeline:

* A pipeline survives `saveRDS()`, so a worker returns the *run pipeline* and
  the app keeps all states: the next run of that pipeline re-runs only outdated
  steps. The returned pipeline holds copies of its outputs, in which ggplots
  get new cache keys, so make figures in such steps with
  `pub_figure(render = TRUE)`: the step then returns the picture, not the plot.
* Computations across groups (e.g. a table of all minima) are steps of the
  report pipeline. Give them the groups' data as parts read with `pub_out()`,
  too.

## Test layout steps

A layout step is a function, and it is easy to test, with two kinds of tests.
Both work on small data, so they run fast.

**The structure.** A layout step references the steps by their names, and
`pip_add()` already rejects a name that does not exist (see above). Run the
pipeline on a small data set and check the document:

```{r test-small, eval = FALSE}
library(testthat)

test_that("the report has the sections and a figure", {
    pip <- report_pipeline() # your constructor
    pip_set_params(pip, list(data = airquality[1:30, ]))
    pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)

    doc <- pip[["report", "out"]]
    expect_s3_class(doc, "pub_doc")
    expect_match(as.character(pub_html(doc)), "Coefficients with 95%")
})
```

**The failures.** A forgotten `~try()` is not an error: it makes the layout
step skip, so the viewer shows no document after a failure. Make a step fail
with a bad param, run on `on_error = "continue"`, and check that the document
is still there and reports the failure:

```{r test-failure}
broken <- pip_clone(pip)
pip_set_params(broken, list(xVar = "Height"))
suppressWarnings(pip_run(broken, on_error = "continue", lgr = NULL))

doc <- broken[["report", "out"]]
class(doc)
grepl("Step 'fit' failed", as.character(pub_html(doc)), fixed = TRUE)
```

As a test:

```{r test-failure-expect, eval = FALSE}
test_that("the report survives a failed fit", {
    pip <- report_pipeline()
    pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Height"))
    suppressWarnings(pip_run(pip, on_error = "continue", lgr = NULL))

    doc <- pip[["report", "out"]]
    expect_s3_class(doc, "pub_doc")
    expect_match(as.character(pub_html(doc)), "Step 'fit' failed", fixed = TRUE)
})
```

For a report that must never be published with a hole in it, test the other
direction: the run with the default `on_error = "stop"` stops, and
`pub_render()` refuses a document with error items:

```{r test-refuse, eval = FALSE}
test_that("a failed step stops the report run", {
    pip <- report_pipeline()
    pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Height"))
    expect_error(pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL), class = "pipeflow_step_error")
})

test_that("pub_render() refuses error items", {
    pip <- report_pipeline()
    pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Height"))
    suppressWarnings(pip_run(pip, on_error = "continue", lgr = NULL))

    expect_error(
        pub_render(pip[["report", "out"]], "docx"),
        class = "pubflow_render_error"
    )
})
```

## Steps that make figures

A ggplot keeps the environment in which it was made: the `aes()` mappings
are quosures that point to the frame of the step, and that frame points to
where the step function was defined. If that is a pipeline constructor, a
figure carries the pipeline and everything the constructor holds, e.g. the
data. As long as the figure stays in the pipeline, nobody notices. It costs as
soon as it travels or lives without its pipeline: a document sent to a worker,
saved with `saveRDS()` or kept by a viewer.

pubflow doesn't check this at run time; the remedy is a habit:

* Write steps that make figures, fits or closures as **top-level functions**
  (in your package or script). Given to `pip_add()` directly (with `params`
  for the `~step` references, as for `coef_table`), neither the figure nor the
  stored step function encloses the constructor. An inline wrapper that only
  calls a top-level helper, as `plot` above, keeps the *figure* free of the
  constructor, but pipeflow stores the wrapper as given, so the saved
  pipeline still holds the constructor's frame.
* Keep step functions out of a function that also holds large data. If a
  constructor takes the data as an argument, steps defined inside it enclose
  that data.
* Let an app test the serialized size of its real documents. The example makes
  the cost visible: a constructor holds 16 MB of data (`big`, used by another
  step) that the figure doesn't show. The same figure is made by a function
  written inline in the constructor and by the top-level `small_plot()`:

```{r size}
small_plot <- function(data) {
    pub_figure(
        ggplot(data, aes(.data$Temp, .data$Ozone)) + geom_point(na.rm = TRUE),
        caption = "Ozone by temperature"
    )
}

make_pipeline <- function(big) {
    pip_new("sizes") |>
        pip_add("data", function(data = airquality) data) |>
        pip_add("other", function(x = big) mean(x)) |>
        pip_add("inline", function(data = ~data) {
            pub_figure(
                ggplot(data, aes(.data$Temp, .data$Ozone)) +
                    geom_point(na.rm = TRUE),
                caption = "Ozone by temperature"
            )
        }) |>
        pip_add("top_level", small_plot, params = list(data = ~data))
}

sizes <- make_pipeline(big = rnorm(2e6))
pip_run(sizes, lgr = NULL)
figures <- sizes[["out"]][c("inline", "top_level")]
round(vapply(figures, \(f) length(serialize(f, NULL)) / 1e6, numeric(1L)), 2) # MB
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
options(old)
```
